config.title: Build typed graph adjacency model

intro.title: Build typed graph adjacency model
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a typed adjacency list model to represent a graph data structure using TypeScript. You will learn how to define a Graph class with type-safe properties for vertices and edges, ensuring your data structures are reliable and error-free. The core programming concept involves using TypeScript's generic types and interfaces to create a flexible and reusable model. By the end, you will have a working graph model that can store connections between nodes with full type checking.
intro.usecase: Typed graph adjacency models are essential for building complex relationship-based features in modern applications. In social networks like Facebook or LinkedIn, they power friend suggestions and connection visualizations by modeling user relationships. E-commerce platforms like Amazon use them for recommendation engines that track "users who bought this also bought" product relationships. Mapping applications like Google Maps rely on adjacency models to represent road networks and calculate optimal routes between locations. Even project management tools use graph models to visualize task dependencies and critical paths in Gantt charts.

objectives: Implement a TypeScript interface to define the structure of a typed graph node.
Construct a generic adjacency list class to manage node connections.
Initialize a typed graph instance with specific node and edge types.
Manipulate the adjacency list by adding and removing nodes and edges.
Apply type constraints to ensure graph operations maintain type safety.
Integrate methods to query adjacency relationships between nodes.
Configure a graph model to represent directed or undirected relationships.

steps.title: Import TypeScript type utilities
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript file and import the Record and Set types from TypeScript's standard library.
steps.hint: Use a named import from 'typescript' to bring in Record and Set.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing types
import { Record, Set } from 'typescript';
steps.seedCode: // Import Record and Set from TypeScript's standard library
steps.expectedOutcome: The file will have the necessary type utilities imported for building a typed graph adjacency model.
successCriteria: Record and Set are imported from 'typescript'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both Record and Set from 'typescript'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. Please import Record and Set from 'typescript'.

steps.title: Define the GraphNode interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named GraphNode with two properties: id (string) and value (generic T).
steps.hint: Use the interface keyword followed by GraphNode<T>. Inside the interface body, specify id: string and value: T.
steps.seedCode:
// Import Record and Set from TypeScript's standard library

// Define the GraphNode interface here
steps.expectedOutcome: An interface GraphNode<T> with id: string and value: T properties is created.
successCriteria: The GraphNode interface is defined with generic type T and contains both id (string) and value (T) properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your interface has both id: string and value: T properties, and uses the generic type T.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Check that you used the interface keyword, named it GraphNode<T>, and included both required properties.

steps.title: Define the Graph interface
steps.instruction: Define an interface named Graph with two properties: nodes (an array of GraphNode<T>) and adjacencyList (a Record<string, Set<string>>).
steps.hint: Use the interface keyword followed by the name Graph, then define the properties with their types inside curly braces.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a Graph interface that describes the structure of your graph with typed nodes and adjacency list.
successCriteria: The Graph interface is defined with nodes: GraphNode<T>[] and adjacencyList: Record<string, Set<string>> properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure both properties (nodes and adjacencyList) are included with the correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Graph interface is missing or has incorrect property types. Review the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Create the createGraph function signature
steps.instruction: Create a function named createGraph with a generic type parameter T that returns a Graph<T>. Write the function signature below the Graph interface.
steps.hint: Start with 'function createGraph<T>(): Graph<T> { }' or use an arrow function. The function should return a Graph<T> object.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named createGraph is defined with a generic type T and returns Graph<T>.
successCriteria: The createGraph function is defined with a generic type parameter T and returns Graph<T>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the function is named createGraph, has a generic type parameter T, and returns Graph<T>.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function signature is incorrect. It should be named createGraph, accept a generic type T, and return Graph<T>.

steps.title: Initialize the graph structure
steps.instruction: Inside the createGraph function, return an object with empty nodes and edges properties that match the Graph<T> interface.
steps.hint: The returned object should have a nodes property set to an empty Record and an edges property set to an empty Record.
steps.expectedOutcome: The createGraph function now returns a properly typed empty graph object.
successCriteria: The createGraph function returns an object with nodes as an empty Record and edges as an empty Record.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure both nodes and edges are set to empty Record objects.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function should return an object matching the Graph<T> interface with empty nodes and edges.

steps.title: Implement the addNode method
steps.instruction: Inside the createGraph function, add an addNode method to the returned graph object that takes a value (type T) and adds a new GraphNode to the nodes record.
steps.hint: The method should generate a unique ID for the node (e.g., using Date.now() or a counter), create a GraphNode object with that ID and the provided value, and store it in the nodes record.
steps.expectedOutcome: The createGraph function returns an object with an addNode method that can add typed nodes to the graph.
successCriteria: The returned graph object includes an addNode method that accepts a value of type T, creates a GraphNode with a unique ID, and stores it in the nodes record.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added the addNode method, but check that it correctly creates a GraphNode and stores it in the nodes record.
steps.feedbackWrong: The addNode method is missing or doesn't properly add a node to the graph. Review the GraphNode interface and the nodes record structure.

steps.title: Implement the getNeighbors method
steps.instruction: Inside the createGraph function, add a getNeighbors method that takes a node ID string and returns the corresponding adjacency Set<string> or an empty Set if the node has no neighbors.
steps.hint: The method should access the edges record using the provided nodeId and return the set found there. If no entry exists, return a new empty Set.
steps.expectedOutcome: The graph object will have a getNeighbors method that retrieves typed adjacency data for any node.
successCriteria: The getNeighbors method is defined inside the returned object, takes a string parameter, and returns a Set<string>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a getNeighbors method, but check the return type and handling of missing nodes.
steps.feedbackWrong: The getNeighbors method is missing or incorrectly implemented. Review the adjacency data structure.

steps.title: Create a sample graph instance
steps.instruction: After the createGraph function, create a graph instance with number type and add three sample nodes with values 10, 20, and 30.
steps.hint: Call createGraph<number>() to create a number-typed graph, then use the addNode method on the returned graph to add nodes.
steps.expectedOutcome: A number-typed graph instance is created and three nodes with values 10, 20, and 30 are added to it.
successCriteria: The code includes a call to createGraph<number>() and three calls to addNode with the values 10, 20, and 30.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created the graph instance, but make sure to add exactly three nodes with values 10, 20, and 30 using addNode.
steps.feedbackWrong: The sample graph instance is not correctly created. Ensure you call createGraph<number>() and add three nodes with the specified values.

steps.title: Add sample edges and test the model
steps.instruction: Inside the sample graph instance, add edges between the existing nodes and call getNeighbors to verify adjacency relationships work correctly.
steps.hint: Use the addEdge method on your graph instance to connect nodes, then call getNeighbors on a node to see its connected neighbors.
steps.expectedOutcome: The sample graph will have edges connecting nodes, and calling getNeighbors will return the correct adjacency list.
successCriteria: Edges are added between sample nodes using addEdge, and getNeighbors is called to verify connections.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've added edges between nodes and called getNeighbors to test the connections.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've added edges between the sample nodes and called getNeighbors to verify adjacency relationships.
